note: Curated herb entries. Traditional use, compound composition and human evidence are kept in SEPARATE fields on purpose and must never be merged when presented. Human evidence cites PMIDs retrieved from PubMed; traditional use cites the ethnobotanical record and is explicitly not clinical evidence.
attribution: Compound and ethnobotanical relationships follow USDA Dr. Duke's Phytochemical and Ethnobotanical Databases (public domain). Human evidence cites PubMed-indexed literature. Safety framing follows NCCIH.

herbs.name: Ginger
traditional_uses: Used traditionally for nausea and motion sickness
Used traditionally for indigestion and digestive discomfort

human_evidence.preparation: powdered ginger / standardised extract, not culinary amounts
human_evidence.summary: Systematic reviews of randomised trials have examined ginger for nausea and vomiting, including pregnancy and post-operative nausea. Findings are generally favourable but trials are small and heterogeneous, and doses studied are higher than typical culinary use.

herbs.safety: Generally well tolerated as a food. May cause mild heartburn. NCCIH notes caution alongside anticoagulant medicines — discuss with a doctor or pharmacist.

herbs.name: Turmeric

human_evidence.preparation: standardised curcumin extract, typically with an absorption enhancer
human_evidence.summary: Trials have studied concentrated curcumin extracts in relation to joint symptoms and inflammatory markers. Results vary and trials are small. Curcumin is poorly absorbed, so this evidence does not transfer to turmeric used as a culinary spice.

herbs.safety: Culinary amounts are widely consumed. Concentrated extracts have been associated with digestive upset and, rarely, liver injury. Discuss extracts with a doctor, particularly alongside anticoagulants.

herbs.name: Garlic
traditional_uses: Used traditionally as a culinary preservative and remedy

human_evidence.preparation: aged garlic extract and garlic powder preparations
human_evidence.summary: Reviews of human trials have examined garlic preparations in relation to blood pressure and blood lipids. Effects reported are modest, trials differ in preparation and dose, and results are not consistent.

herbs.safety: Common as a food. May increase bleeding risk with anticoagulants, and can cause digestive upset and odour. Discuss supplements with a doctor before surgery.

herbs.name: Peppermint
traditional_uses: Used traditionally for digestive discomfort and bloating
Used traditionally as a tea after meals

human_evidence.preparation: enteric-coated peppermint oil capsules, not tea
human_evidence.summary: Human trials have studied enteric-coated peppermint oil in irritable bowel syndrome symptoms. This evidence concerns a specific capsule preparation and does not apply to peppermint tea or culinary use.

herbs.safety: Peppermint tea is widely consumed. Oil capsules can cause heartburn and are not suitable for everyone; discuss with a doctor if you have reflux or gallbladder problems.

herbs.name: Cinnamon
traditional_uses: Used traditionally as a warming digestive spice

human_evidence.preparation: cinnamon powder and extracts at supplement doses
human_evidence.summary: Reviews of human trials examining cinnamon and blood glucose report inconsistent findings, with substantial differences between trials in species, dose and duration.

herbs.safety: Culinary amounts are widely consumed. Cassia cinnamon contains coumarin, which in large regular supplement doses has been linked to liver concerns; Ceylon cinnamon contains far less.

herbs.name: Rosemary
traditional_uses: Used traditionally as a culinary and preservative herb
Used traditionally in preparations associated with alertness
herbs.safety: Culinary amounts are widely consumed. Concentrated oils should not be taken internally without professional advice.

herbs.name: Chamomile
traditional_uses: Used traditionally as a calming tea before sleep

human_evidence.summary: Small human trials have examined chamomile preparations in relation to sleep quality and anxiety symptoms. Trials are small and results are preliminary.

herbs.safety: Generally well tolerated. People allergic to plants in the daisy family may react. Discuss with a doctor alongside anticoagulants or sedatives.

herbs.name: Green tea
traditional_uses: Consumed traditionally as a daily beverage across East Asia

human_evidence.preparation: brewed tea and green tea extracts
human_evidence.summary: Pooled analyses of human trials have examined green tea consumption in relation to blood lipids. Reported changes are small, and extract studies differ substantially from drinking tea.

human_evidence.preparation: brewed tea and L-theanine plus caffeine combinations
human_evidence.summary: Trials have examined the combination of L-theanine and caffeine found in tea in relation to attention on short tasks. Effects are small and short-term.

herbs.safety: Drinking tea is widely considered safe. High-dose concentrated extracts have been associated with liver injury in rare cases; NCCIH advises caution with extracts.

herbs.name: Maca
traditional_uses: Used traditionally in the Andes as a food and tonic root

human_evidence.preparation: dried maca powder at supplement doses
human_evidence.summary: Small randomised trials have examined maca powder in relation to self-reported sexual desire. Trials are few and small, and results have not been consistently replicated.

herbs.safety: Eaten as a food in Peru. Generally well tolerated; data in pregnancy and in thyroid conditions is limited, so discuss with a doctor.

herbs.name: Fenugreek
traditional_uses: Used traditionally as a culinary spice and in tonic preparations

human_evidence.preparation: standardised fenugreek seed extract, not culinary amounts
human_evidence.summary: Small trials of standardised fenugreek extracts have reported changes in self-reported sexual function and some hormonal measures. Trials are small, often industry-funded, and this does not apply to fenugreek used as a spice.

herbs.safety: Common as a spice. Extracts may lower blood sugar and can interact with diabetes medicines and anticoagulants; discuss with a doctor. Avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy.

herbs.name: Ginseng
traditional_uses: Used traditionally in East Asia as a tonic root for fatigue and vitality

human_evidence.summary: Systematic reviews of small randomised trials have examined Panax ginseng extracts in relation to erectile function and fatigue. The authors note that trials are small and of limited methodological quality.

herbs.safety: May cause insomnia and headache. Can interact with anticoagulants, diabetes medicines and some antidepressants; discuss with a doctor or pharmacist before use.

herbs.name: Sage
traditional_uses: Used traditionally as a culinary herb and in preparations associated with memory

human_evidence.preparation: sage extract capsules, not culinary amounts
human_evidence.summary: Small short-term trials have examined sage extracts in relation to attention and memory task performance in healthy adults. Studies are small and effects are modest and short-lived.

herbs.safety: Culinary amounts are widely consumed. Sage oil contains thujone, which is not safe in large or prolonged doses; avoid medicinal doses in pregnancy and in seizure disorders.
